'''Mary Lisa Manning''' (born 1980) is an American [[physicist]] and the [[William R. Kenan, Jr.]], Professor<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=M. Lisa Manning, professor of physics and founding director of BioInspired Syracuse: Institute for Material and Living Systems, has been named the William R. Kenan, Jr., Professor of Physics. This highly selective professorship was established in 1971 by|url=https://thecollege.syr.edu/news-all/news-2020/m-lisa-manning-named-william-r-kenan-jr-professor-physics/|access-date=2020-06-22|website=College of Arts & Sciences at Syracuse University|language=en-us}}</ref> of Physics at [[Syracuse University]] in [[Syracuse, New York]], United States. Manning's research focuses on the behavior of glassy materials, using [[simulations]] and [[theory]] to model the emergent properties of [[biological tissues]].

==Background==

Manning grew up in Kentucky, near [[Cincinnati, Ohio]] and attended the [[University of Virginia]] as a [[Jefferson Scholar]], graduating in 2002 with bachelor's degrees in physics and mathematics.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.jeffersonscholars.org/people/lisa-manning|title=Lisa Manning - Jefferson Scholars Foundation|website=www.jeffersonscholars.org}}</ref><ref name="on leadership"/> She earned a Ph.D. in physics from the [[University of California at Santa Barbara]] in 2008, followed by a [[postdoctoral fellowship]] at the [[Princeton University]] Center for Theoretical Science. In 2011, Manning accepted a faculty position at [[Syracuse University]]. In 2020, Manning was named the [[William R. Kenan, Jr.]], Professor<ref name=":0" /> of Physics at the same university.

Manning is married to William Wylie and has two children.<ref name="on leadership">{{cite news |last1=Morelli |first1=Marie |title=M. Lisa Manning on leadership: Give people 'the freedom to work on things and the freedom to fail' |url=https://www.syracuse.com/business/2024/06/m-lisa-manning-on-leadership-give-people-the-freedom-to-work-on-things-and-the-freedom-to-fail.html |access-date=19 June 2024 |work=[[syracuse.com]] |date=19 June 2024 |language=en}}</ref>

==Research==

As a graduate student, Manning studied the behaviors and properties of disordered solids and [[glass]]es under the mentorship of Jean Carlson. Among other findings, she described how effective temperature is an important determinant of material failure and [[Deformation (mechanics)|strain]] localization, with potential applications for a wide range of [[amorphous materials]].<ref>{{Cite thesis |degree=PhD |title= Effective temperature and strain localization in amorphous solids |url=https://search.library.ucsb.edu/discovery/fulldisplay?vid=01UCSB_INST:UCSB&tab=Everything&docid=alma990033037010203776&context=L&search_scope=DN_and_CI&lang=en |access-date=2022-09-01 |isbn=978-0-549-84257-6 |publisher=University of California, Santa Barbara |language=en}}</ref>

After earning her Ph.D., Manning expanded her research on amorphous and granular solids to include [[biological cells]], noting that many types of [[Tissue (biology)|tissues]] behave as though they were glassy solids.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/the-physics-of-glass-opens-a-window-into-biology-20180611/|title=The Physics of Glass Opens a Window Into Biology - Quanta Magazine|date=11 June 2018|publisher=}}</ref> Manning has developed a [[Mathematical model|model]] describing the relationship between [[cell adhesion]] and cortical tension as a determinant for [[embryo]]nic [[surface tension]].<ref>{{cite journal | first1=M. Lisa | last1=Manning | title=Coaction of intercellular adhesion and cortical tension specifies tissue surface tension | date=13 July 2010 | last2=Foty | first2=Ramsey A. | last3=Steinberg | first3=Malcolm S. | last4=Schoetz | first4=Eva-Maria | journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences | volume=107 | issue=28 | pages=12517–12522 | doi=10.1073/pnas.1003743107 | pmid=20616053 | pmc=2906578 | bibcode=2010PNAS..10712517M | doi-access=free }}</ref> Her ongoing research modeling the relationship between cell shape and [[Jamming (physics)|jamming]] leading to tissue rigidity has implications for [[cell migration]] in [[metastatic cancer]], [[wound healing]], [[embryogenesis]], and [[asthma]].<ref>{{Cite journal |arxiv = 1706.02656|last1 = Merkel|first1 = Matthias|title = A geometrically controlled rigidity transition in a model for confluent 3D tissues|journal = New Journal of Physics|volume = 20|issue = 2|page = 022002|last2 = Manning|first2 = Lisa|year = 2017|doi = 10.1088/1367-2630/aaaa13|s2cid = 3867697}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |arxiv = 1308.3891|last1 = Merkel|first1 = Matthias|title = Energy barriers govern glassy dynamics in tissues|journal = Soft Matter|volume = 10|issue = 12|pages = 1885–90|last2 = Manning|first2 = Lisa|last3 = Schwarz|first3 = J. M.|author3-link=Jennifer Schwarz|last4 = Manning|first4 = M. Lisa|year = 2013|doi = 10.1039/c3sm52893f|pmid = 24652538}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Knowing the Boundaries: Extending the Differential Adhesion Hypothesis in Embryonic Cell Sorting|first1=Jeffrey D.|last1=Amack|first2=M.
